note: Each mutation is a CONCRETE PATCH -- file, an anchor that must occur exactly once, and its replacement -- never a sentence describing an edit. A sentence cannot be replayed. `node scripts/mutate.mjs run` applies each in an isolated tree archived from HEAD, enforces the four kill rules, and writes the `observed` record itself; nothing in this file is typed by hand except the patch and the kill it names. See scripts/mutate.mjs and audits/_MASTER-TEMPLATE.md section 4.1c.

kills.rule1: the owning test PASSED unmutated in the same run
kills.rule2: the patch actually CHANGED the file (anchor unique, bytes different, round trip clean)
kills.rule3: the run served the MUTATED code -- the built bundle's hash moved, AND the failure does not match a shape that means the code never ran
kills.rule4: the failure is that marker's OWN named assertion, not the suite going red

classical-match-inverted.why: Panel 1's verdict is the page's answer to 'did both sides get the same secret?'. Inverting the measurement makes the page report a mismatch while printing two identical secret prefixes directly above it. The claims test cross-checks those two surfaces, so this is the mutation that proves the cross-check is doing work rather than agreeing with the source.

size-ratio-inverted.why: Size is the only comparison this lab makes, chosen because a beginner can check it with division. Swapping the division gives 0 instead of 35.5 while every byte count on the page stays correct -- so only a test that does the division ITSELF, over the two totals on screen, can catch it. A test that re-used the source's expression would have agreed with the bug.

byte-flip-noop.why: Panel 3 claims a byte was changed and that the two sides then hold different secrets. This patch leaves the ciphertext untouched while the panel goes on saying a byte was changed -- the exact shape of a lab that tells rather than shows. The claims test re-derives the difference from the two prefixes the verdict quotes, so a page merely asserting it cannot pass.

impostor-uses-raes-key.why: This breaks a check INSIDE the negative claim's evidence fixture, which section 4.1d requires: with the impostor's key pair quietly being Rae's own, the exchange really does reach Rae and the fixture is no longer evidence of anything. The verdict is computed from the MEASURED raeHoldsTheSecret rather than from the option the reader picked, which is the only reason this is visible on the page at all. The patch rebinds `mal` rather than rewriting the ternary that reads it: `impostor ? rae : rae` leaves `mal` unused and noUnusedLocals makes that DOES NOT BUILD, which proves nothing -- the first version of this record was exactly that, and the runner said so.

panel-1-retires-panel-3.why: Section 4.1b's no-op guard, inverted: panel 1 is a different exchange, so running it must leave panel 3's conclusion standing. This patch makes an unrelated action throw away a verdict the reader is still reading. The comment it adds the call beneath is left in place deliberately, so the mutated source reads as self-contradictory rather than plausible.

size-bar-not-to-scale.why: The bars are new, and a chart is a new way to get a ratio wrong that a reader has no way to check. This patch floors every bar at 40% of the track, which makes the 64-byte bar look roughly a third as long as the 2,272-byte one instead of a fortieth -- while every printed number, the quotient and the verdict all stay correct. A reader who trusts the picture is told something between 10 and 20 times wrong by a page that is otherwise honest. Only a test that reads the PAINTED widths back and divides them can see it, which is why the claims test measures getBoundingClientRect rather than the style attribute it would be re-deriving.
